q: The phrase "form follows function" is attributed to
n: "Form (ever) follows function" comes from Louis Sullivan (1896). Source: Sullivan, "The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered" (1896).

q: The quote "One of the great beauties of architecture is that each time, it's like life starting all over again" speaks of the continued rebirth of creativity. To whom is this attributed?
n: "One of the great beauties of architecture is that each time, it's like life starting all over again" is by Renzo Piano. Source: Renzo Piano Building Workshop; Pritzker acceptance (1998).

q: A house is a machine for living in
n: "A house is a machine for living in" is from Le Corbusier (Charles-Édouard Jeanneret), Vers une architecture (1923). Source: Le Corbusier, Towards a New Architecture.

q: Who said: "Architecture is not based on concrete and steel, and the elements of the soil. It is based on wonder."?
n: "Architecture is not based on concrete and steel and the elements of the soil. It's based on wonder" is by Daniel Libeskind. Source: Studio Libeskind; Libeskind, Breaking Ground (2004).

q: Minimalism is exemplified by the idea of "less is more". This approach Involves stripping a design down to its bare essentials, and casting aside any elements that Co not contribute to the pure beauty or function of an object or space, It aims to create spaces that are serene, time less and free from distractions, emphasizing clarity and purpose. Who first coined this phrase?
n: "Less is more" is the motto of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. (Robert Browning used the phrase earlier in poetry.) Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: The phrase "less is a bore" was a challenge and a rebuke of the result of the architecture of minimalism, and a return to a more interesting mannerist approach to design.
n: Robert Venturi's "Less is a bore" rebuked minimalist Modernism. Source: Venturi, Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966).

q: The quote "Architecture must have something that appeals to the human heart. Creative work is expressed in our time as a union of technology and humanity Nevertheless, tho basic farms, spaces, and appearances must be logical" is attributed to?
n: The quote on architecture appealing to the human heart as a union of technology and humanity is Kenzo Tange's. Source: Tange, Pritzker acceptance (1987).

q: The statement "The mother art is architecture. Without an architecture of our own we have no soul of our own civilization" reflects a philosophy that places architecture at the center of cultural identity. It comes from an architect whose work championed organic architecture, the integration of buildings with their natural surroundings, and a uniquely American architectural language expressed in works such as Fallingwater, the Robie House, and the Guggenheim Museum. Which architect is credited with this statement?
n: "The mother art is architecture..." is Frank Lloyd Wright's. Source: Wright, An Autobiography; Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation.

q: The quote "In all my works, light is an important controlling factor" is attributed to?
n: "In all my works, light is an important controlling factor" is Tadao Ando's. Source: Ando, Pritzker acceptance (1995).

q: Which architect, renowned for minimalist concrete architecture and the expressive use of natural light and shadow, is associated with the statement "Light is the origin of all being"?
n: Tadao Ando, known for minimalist concrete and light, is associated with "Light is the origin of all being." Source: Ando, Pritzker acceptance (1995).

q: Who said: "Architecture is a learned game, correct and magnificent, of forms assembled in the light"?
n: "Architecture is the learned game, correct and magnificent, of forms assembled in the light" is Le Corbusier's. Source: Le Corbusier, Towards a New Architecture (1923).

q: Who is the architect who said "An idea is salvation by imagination"?
n: "An idea is salvation by imagination" is Frank Lloyd Wright's. Source: Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation (quotations).

q: Who said "Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication"?
n: "Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication" is commonly attributed to Leonardo da Vinci. Source: Quote attribution references (Leonardo da Vinci).

q: The quotation "To create, one must first question everything" is associated with which influential figure whose work helped shape early Modernist architecture and furniture design?
n: "To create, one must first question everything" is attributed to Eileen Gray, the modernist architect and furniture designer. Source: Eileen Gray archives (Centre Pompidou); Constant, Eileen Gray (2000).

q: Who said: "The purpose of architecture is to shelter and enhance man's life on earth and to fulfill his belief in the nobility of his existence"?
n: "The purpose of architecture is to shelter and enhance man's life on earth and to fulfill his belief in the nobility of his existence" is Eero Saarinen's. Source: Eero Saarinen on His Work (1962).

q: The phrase "As an architect, you design for the present, with an awareness of the past, fora future which is essentially unknown," was coined by?
n: "As an architect you design for the present, with an awareness of the past, for a future which is essentially unknown" is Norman Foster's. Source: Foster + Partners; Foster, Pritzker acceptance (1999).

q: "For our father, every line must have a meaning, a purpose. For him, function comes first before elegance or form" was a phrase popularized hy?
n: Pablo Antonio's children described their father's credo that every line must have meaning and that function comes before elegance. Source: NCCA, National Artist Pablo S. Antonio.

q: The following are attributed to Zaha Hadid except
o: When I'm working on a problem, I never think about beauty. But when I'm finished, if the solution is not beautiful, I know it's wrong.
I don't think that architecture is only about shelter, only about a very simple enclosure. It should be able to excite you, to calm you, to make you think.
There are 360 degrees, so why stick to one?
Architecture is like writing. You have to edit it over and over so it looks effortless.
n: "When I'm working on a problem, I never think about beauty..." is by Buckminster Fuller, not Zaha Hadid. The others are Hadid's. Source: Buckminster Fuller Institute; Zaha Hadid Architects.

q: The following are attributed to Le Corbusier except
o: Architecture is a learned game, correct and magnificent, of forms assembled in the light.
My buildings are more famous than me.
I prefer drawing to talking. Drawing is faster and leaves less room for lies.
Light creates ambiance and feel of a place, as well as the expression of a structure.
n: "Light creates ambiance and feel of a place, as well as the expression of a structure" is Le Corbusier's. It is often quoted. Source: Le Corbusier quotations (Fondation Le Corbusier).

q: Gorge cornice
n: The gorge (cavetto) cornice is characteristic of Egyptian architecture. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Egyptian Architecture.

q: Gorge moldings
n: Gorge moldings are Egyptian. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Egyptian Architecture.

q: Battered walls with no windows
n: Battered (inward-sloping) walls without windows are Egyptian. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Egyptian Architecture.

q: Fluted column with vertical scrolls
n: Fluted columns with vertical double-scroll (volute) capitals belong to West Asiatic (Persian) architecture, as at Persepolis. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), West Asiatic Architecture.

q: Fluted column with double-animal capital
n: Fluted columns with double-animal (bull) capitals are Persian (West Asiatic), as at Persepolis. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), West Asiatic Architecture.

q: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian
n: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian are the Greek orders. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Greek Architecture.

q: Tuscan and Composite
n: The Romans added Tuscan and Composite to the orders. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Roman Architecture.

q: Vaulted Ceilings
n: Vaulted ceilings, built of concrete and brick, are a hallmark of Roman architecture. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Roman Architecture.

q: Art movement that combined modernist style with fine craftsmanship and rich materials, drawing on many different styles in architecture
n: Art Deco combined modern style with fine craftsmanship and rich materials, drawing on many earlier styles. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: An architectural style that emphasizes geometry, symmetry, and regularity of parts.
n: Renaissance architecture stresses geometry, symmetry and regularity of parts. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Renaissance Architecture.

q: This design movement was popular from 1890 to 1910 throughout Europe and the United States. It is characterized by organic lines, intricate patterns and earthy colors. The structures tend to be asymmetrical, often using materials like concrete, metal and glass.
n: Art Nouveau (about 1890–1910) has organic lines, intricate patterns and asymmetry, using iron, glass and concrete. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Architectural style which is the reintroduction of Classical elements
n: The Renaissance reintroduced Classical elements. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Renaissance Architecture.

q: A popular design style characterized by sleek geometric or stylized forms. Its buildings often used stucco, chrome, steel, decorative glass, terracotta and aluminum.
n: Art Deco has sleek geometric or stylized forms in stucco, chrome, steel, decorative glass, terracotta and aluminum. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: The most common characteristics of this style are rectilinear forms, light, taut plane surfaces stripped of ornamentation and decoration, a visually weightless quality, and open interior spaces engendered by the use of cantilever construction. Philip Johnson described this style as plain, unadorned architecture of rectilinear forms built of steel, reinforced concrete and glass.
n: Hitchcock and Johnson defined the International Style as plain rectilinear forms of steel, concrete and glass, stripped of ornament. Source: Hitchcock & Johnson, The International Style (1932).

q: Which early 20th-century design movement is widely regarded as a precursor to Minimalist architecture due to its emphasis on geometric abstraction, visual order, simplicity, and reduction of form?
n: De Stijl, with geometric abstraction, order and reduction, is a precursor of Minimalist architecture. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History.

q: To promote visual continuity, spatial flexibility, and a sense of openness, minimalist architecture most commonly favors which planning approach?
o: Hierarchical room arrangements emphasizing formal boundaries
Radial planning organized around a central hall
Open floor plans with minimal partitions
Specifically designed spaces separated by numerous enclosed rooms
n: Minimalist architecture favors open floor plans with few partitions, for continuity and flexibility. Source: Pawson, Minimum (1996).

q: The expressive stainless-steel exterior and seemingly fragmented, non-orthogonal forms of Frank Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall exemplify which architectural movement?
n: Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall, with fragmented non-orthogonal steel forms, is Deconstructivist. Source: Frampton, Modern Architecture: A Critical History; MoMA, Deconstructivist Architecture (1988).

q: In minimalist architecture, ornamentation is minimized and architectural space and volume must be defined through essential design elements. Which element is most effective in shaping the perception of space and volume while maintaining a minimalist aesthetic?
n: In minimalist architecture, natural light is the most effective element for shaping space and volume. Source: Pawson, Minimum; Ando, writings on light.

q: It has a frilly style replete with serpentine curves, spirals and undulations. Stucco was a common material used as it could be molded to a shape and design to awe the viewer. Bright pastel colors were another element of this style.
n: Rococo is frilly, with serpentine curves, molded stucco and pastel colors. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.); Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: This architectural style, which originated in Italy in the 17th century, is highly opulent and ornate. It is characterized by curved and dynamic forms, gilded ornamentation and bright colors, and employed optical effects such as trompe-l'oeil and light and shadow. Stucco and marble were extensively used, and the scale was grand and monumental.
n: Baroque, from 17th-century Italy, is opulent: dynamic curves, gilding, trompe-l'oeil, stucco and marble at grand scale. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Baroque Architecture.

q: Gothic architecture is characterized by
n: Gothic is characterized both by pointed arches and by intricate detail (tracery, sculpture). Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Gothic Architecture.

q: The pointed arch is a defining characteristic of which architectural style?
n: The pointed arch is the defining feature of Gothic. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Gothic Architecture.

q: Which type of door is directly inspired by the pointed arches and ornate tracery of church window styles—emphasizing verticality, spiritual symbolism, and medieval craftsmanship?
n: Gothic doors take the pointed arches and tracery of church windows. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: Predominant architectural style of the 16th century
n: The Renaissance was the dominant style of the 16th century. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Renaissance Architecture.

q: An architectural style characterized by the use of shells and curves which emerged in 18" century France and is known for its elaborate ornamentation, asymmetrical designs, pastel colors, lightness, the use of gold leaf for decoration anc elegance. It favors a more playful and intimate aesthetic.
n: Rococo (18th-century France) has shell and curve motifs, asymmetry, pastels, gold leaf and a playful lightness. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.); Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Fletcher, A History of Architecture.

q: An architectural style that emerged in the late Italian Renaissance around 1520, characterized by its departure from the harmonious and balanced principles of the High Renaissance and its complexity, tension and novelty. Notable examples include the Palazzo del Te by Giulio Romano and the Laurentian Library by Michelangelo.
n: Mannerism (from about 1520) broke High Renaissance harmony with complexity and tension, as in Palazzo del Te and the Laurentian Library. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Renaissance Architecture in Italy.

q: The Florence Baptistery in Italy, also known as the Baptistery of Saint John, was built in what style?
n: The Florence Baptistery of St. John is Florentine Romanesque. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Romanesque Architecture in Italy.

q: It has been called the most spectacular endeavor of the English medieval carpenter.
n: The hammerbeam roof (as at Westminster Hall) is called the most spectacular work of the English medieval carpenter. Source: Fletcher, A History of Architecture (20th ed.), Gothic Architecture in England.
